title: India and the EU Just Signed the Biggest Free Trade Deal in History. It Took 20 Years.
excerpt: The 'mother of all deals' creates a free trade zone of 2 billion people, slashes car tariffs from 110% to 10%, and reshapes India's position in a fracturing global trade order.
body:
It took nearly two decades of starts, stops, and bureaucratic inertia. But on Tuesday, India and the European Union finally signed what both sides are calling the most ambitious free trade agreement either has ever concluded — a deal that creates a free trade zone covering 2 billion people, a quarter of the world's GDP, and roughly a third of global trade.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, landing in New Delhi alongside European Council President António Costa, called it "the mother of all deals." Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, standing beside her at the India-EU summit, said it would bring "massive opportunities for 1.4 billion Indians and millions of people in European countries."

## Why It Matters Now

The deal's timing is not accidental. Both India and the EU are facing punitive tariffs from the United States under President Donald Trump's administration — India at 50% on exports, and the EU under threat over its objections to Trump's designs on Greenland. Meanwhile, both are trying to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing and find new supply chain partners.

Trade talks between New Delhi and Brussels began in 2007 but collapsed over disputes on agriculture, dairy, and automobile access. They were revived in 2022 and accelerated dramatically over the past six months. The final text was agreed late on Monday night.

## What Changes

The numbers are stark. India will slash tariffs on European cars from 110% to as low as 10% over five years, with a quota allowing up to 250,000 European-made vehicles to enter at preferential rates — far more than the 37,000-vehicle limit under India's recent UK deal. Tariffs on car parts will be fully eliminated within five to ten years.

For European companies, the EU estimates €4 billion a year in tariff savings. The deal eliminates or reduces duties on 96.6% of traded goods by value. Machinery, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals from Europe will see significant tariff cuts. Wine and spirits will become cheaper for Indian consumers.

In return, India gains easier access to European markets for textiles, gems, and pharmaceuticals — sectors where it already has competitive strength but faces non-tariff barriers. The deal also covers services, where Indian IT and business process firms stand to benefit from simplified market access across 27 countries.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the roughly 2 million Indians living and working across Europe, the deal carries practical implications. A mobility pact folded into the broader EU-India strategic agenda promises easier visa processes for business travelers and professionals. Indian pharmaceutical exports to Europe — already a $10 billion market — could grow substantially as regulatory alignment improves.

For NRIs in the US watching European car brands become more accessible back home, the deal also reshapes the economics of gifting, shipping, and family purchases. A BMW or Volkswagen in India could cost 30-40% less within five years under the new tariff schedule.

## What Comes Next

The formal signing ceremony is expected later this year, with implementation beginning as early as 2027. The tariff reductions will be phased over 5 to 10 years, giving Indian manufacturers time to adjust.

But the real significance may be geopolitical. The EU-India FTA is widely seen as the clearest signal yet of a post-American trade architecture taking shape — one where major democracies hedge against Washington's unpredictability by building bilateral ties that bypass the US entirely.

"This is not just a trade deal," said one EU trade official, speaking on background. "This is about showing the world that multilateral, rules-based commerce has a future, even if the largest economy on earth has decided to walk away from it."

Whether India's domestic manufacturers — particularly in the auto sector — can survive the competitive pressure is the question that will define the deal's legacy. For now, New Delhi is betting that access to 450 million wealthy European consumers is worth the disruption at home.
author: Diaspora Desk
